What was life like in Tenochtitlan during the Aztec Empire?
a: Life in Tenochtitlan at its peak in the 15th and early 16th centuries was a vibrant, cosmopolitan experience centered around the city's canals, markets, and grand architecture. Built on an island in Lake Texcoco, the city was home to an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 people, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time. Residents navigated the city by canoe along a network of canals and causeways, with merchants transporting goods in elaborate dugout canoes. The city's main market, Tlatelolco, was one of the largest markets in the Americas, where traders from across the Aztec Empire sold everything from cacao beans and textiles to exotic feathers and slaves. Social stratification was strict — the emperor and nobility lived in grand stone palaces with elaborate gardens and temples, while commoners lived in crowded, one-room houses made of adobe and thatch. The city's architecture was impressive, with the Templo Mayor rising over the main plaza, its twin temples dedicated to the gods Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. Daily life revolved around agriculture, with chinampas (floating gardens) producing multiple crops of maize, beans, and squash. Food was central to Aztec culture — commoners ate maize, beans, squash, and chili peppers, while the wealthy enjoyed turkey, fish, and exotic game. Education was highly valued: children from noble families attended the calmecac (house of the young) to learn history, religion, and governance, while commoner children learned practical skills. Religion permeated every aspect of life, with elaborate ceremonies, human sacrifices, and festivals marking the agricultural calendar. The city had advanced engineering, including an aqueduct that brought fresh water from the mainland and a system of dykes to protect against flooding. Despite its grandeur, life was harsh for most residents — disease, warfare, and heavy taxation were constant threats. The arrival of Spanish conquistadors in 1519 brought devastating epidemics that killed much of the population, and the city was destroyed in 1521 during the Spanish conquest.
